title: You Can Be Faithful in Church and Unfaithful in Your Imagination
paragraphs: You Can Be Faithful in Church and Unfaithful in Your Imagination
You may never touch another person. You may never send the message. You may never cross the physical line. And still, Jesus loves you too much to leave the secret rooms of your imagination untouched.
There is a kind of unfaithfulness that leaves no lipstick on a collar.
No suspicious hotel receipt.
No hidden second phone.
No unfamiliar perfume.
No confession beginning with, “Something happened.”
Sometimes there is nothing for a spouse to discover because everything happened behind the eyes.
You went to church.
You sang the worship songs.
You opened your Bible.
You greeted people in the lobby.
You came home to the person you promised to love.
And nobody knew where your imagination had been.
That sentence may hurt.
But perhaps it needs to.
Because Jesus once spoke to people who knew how to measure sexual faithfulness by what the body had done, and then He moved the boundary deeper.
Into the heart.
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I tell you that anyone who looks at a woman lustfully has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
—Matthew 5:27–28
The Greek makes the force of His words difficult to escape.
“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν”
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn.
The issue is not merely that the human eye noticed another human being.
Jesus was not teaching that recognizing beauty is adultery.
He was not saying that every involuntary temptation, unwanted thought, intrusive image, or momentary attraction means you have already committed adultery.
That distinction matters enormously, especially to believers tormented by unwanted thoughts.
The wording points toward looking with the purpose or direction of lusting—the gaze that does not merely encounter desire but welcomes it, feeds it, returns to it, and gives it somewhere to live.
There is a difference between temptation knocking at the door and pulling up a chair for it.
There is a difference between noticing and nurturing.
Between an unwanted thought and an entertained fantasy.
Between being tempted and deliberately turning another person into material for your private sexual imagination.
Jesus goes after that distinction because Jesus is not interested merely in producing people who appear sexually faithful.
He wants hearts that are becoming faithful.
And that is where this gets painfully personal.
You can remain physically faithful while secretly rehearsing betrayal.
You can sleep beside your spouse while fantasizing about somebody else.
You can celebrate an anniversary while repeatedly visiting images you would panic to have projected onto the wall.
You can delete your browsing history and still carry the history in your imagination.
You can know exactly which accounts trigger you.
Exactly which scenes you replay.
Exactly which person you enjoy imagining.
Exactly when your spouse leaves the room.
Exactly when you reach for the phone.
And you can become frighteningly skilled at keeping all of it invisible.
No affair.
No physical touch.
No public scandal.
So you tell yourself:
“At least I never cheated.”
And Jesus asks a more penetrating question:
What is your heart learning to desire?
That is the hidden territory of faithfulness we rarely want to discuss.
Because physical boundaries are easier to measure.
The imagination has no witnesses.
Except God.
And perhaps that is why secret lust can survive for years inside outwardly respectable Christianity.
You can serve while hiding it.
Preach while hiding it.
Lead worship while hiding it.
Teach Bible study while hiding it.
Post Scripture while hiding it.
Hold your spouse’s hand in church while hiding it.
Nobody sees the private movie.
Nobody hears the internal dialogue.
Nobody knows how often you revisit the fantasy.
Nobody knows how much comparison has entered your marriage.
But Jesus does.
And remarkably, He still came for people like us.
That is where conviction must never be separated from the Gospel.
Because if all you hear in Matthew 5 is, “You are disgusting,” you have not yet heard the full voice of Christ.
Jesus exposes darkness because He came to rescue people from darkness.
He names sin because sin destroys what He loves.
The same Christ who says lust matters is the Christ who goes to the cross for lustful people.
The same Savior who exposes the heart offers to cleanse it.
Christianity is not the story of clean people standing far away from dirty people.
It is the story of sinners discovering that the Son of God came near.
Maybe your struggle has been pornography.
Maybe it has been someone at work.
Maybe it is an ex you keep resurrecting in your imagination.
Maybe it is a fictional person.
Maybe it is endless scrolling because you already know what kind of content the algorithm will eventually place before you.
Maybe you would never message the person whose pictures you repeatedly revisit.
Maybe your spouse has absolutely no idea.
Maybe you are single and have convinced yourself that faithfulness does not apply until marriage.
But sexual holiness is not merely loyalty to a present or future spouse.
It is first loyalty to Christ.
Paul wrote:
“Flee from sexual immorality.”
—1 Corinthians 6:18
Not negotiate with it.
Not domesticate it.
Not keep it close enough to enjoy while promising yourself you will never go “too far.”
Flee.
Why?
Because your body does not ultimately belong to your appetites.
“You are not your own; you were bought at a price. Therefore honor God with your bodies.”
—1 Corinthians 6:19–20
Bought.
At a price.
That changes the conversation.
Christian purity is not primarily about becoming impressive enough for God.
It is the response of someone who realizes:
Christ purchased me.
Christ loves me.
Christ died for me.
Christ rose for me.
I belong to Him.
So perhaps the question is no longer merely:
“How far can I go before this becomes sin?”
Perhaps the better question is:
“How completely can I belong to Jesus?”
That question reaches places religious performance never will.
It reaches the browser history.
The saved pictures.
The private messages.
The television choices.
The fantasies before sleep.
The person you deliberately look for across the room.
The comparison you keep making between your spouse and somebody else.
The memory you keep sexualizing.
The secret account.
The second glance.
The third glance.
The thought you could have released but chose instead to develop.
And suddenly holiness stops being a list of forbidden physical acts.
It becomes love.
Because if you are married, the person beside you deserves more than technical fidelity.
They deserve a heart continually being surrendered to Christ.
And whether married or single, the people you encounter are not bodies placed on earth for your consumption.
They bear the image of God.
They are somebody’s daughter.
Somebody’s son.
Somebody Christ calls you to regard with dignity rather than reduce to fantasy.
Lust asks:
“What can I take from this person in my imagination?”
Love asks:
“How can I see this person as God sees them?”
That battle may happen in seconds.
And sometimes you will lose.
That needs to be said too.
Because someone reading this has already failed so many times that another purity article feels like another stone being placed on your chest.
You promised God.
Failed.
Cried.
Deleted everything.
Returned.
Confessed.
Failed again.
Maybe you have wondered whether your repentance can possibly be real if the battle keeps returning.
Listen carefully.
Repeated temptation does not mean Christ has abandoned you.
But repeated surrender to sin should never be renamed harmless because you are tired of fighting it.
Grace does not tell you to make peace with the chains.
Grace opens the prison door.
Scripture says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just and will forgive us our sins and purify us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9
Notice who is faithful when we have been unfaithful.
He is.
Jesus is.
Your hope is not that your record suddenly becomes flawless.
Your hope is that Christ’s mercy is greater than the record you bring Him—and that His grace does not merely pardon you but begins transforming you.
Repentance means you stop protecting what Jesus is asking you to surrender.
Maybe that means confessing to God without euphemisms.
Maybe it means removing an app.
Unfollowing someone.
Installing accountability.
Moving the phone out of the bedroom.
Stopping the private conversation you keep pretending is innocent.
Talking to a mature believer.
Seeking pastoral counsel.
Having an appropriately honest conversation in your marriage.
Getting help when pornography or compulsive sexual behavior has become deeply entrenched.
Not because external safeguards can manufacture holiness.
They cannot.
But sometimes repentance looks remarkably practical.
Jesus did not die so you could become better at hiding.
He died to bring you into the light.
And the light may feel terrifying when you have lived in secrecy.
But secrecy has been charging you rent.
It takes peace.
Intimacy.
Confidence in prayer.
Tenderness toward your spouse.
Clarity of conscience.
Sometimes even your ability to look another human being in the eyes without internally turning them into something they were never meant to become.
Eventually the hidden room stops feeling like freedom.
It becomes a cell.
And Jesus stands at the door calling you out.
Not into humiliation.
Into freedom.
This is the scandal of grace.
Jesus already knows the version of you that you are desperately trying to keep everyone else from seeing.
And He still calls you to Himself.
Not so you can remain unchanged.
So He can remake you.
That is why the Gospel is infinitely better than image management.
Image management says:
“Make sure nobody finds out.”
The Gospel says:
“Come into the light.”
Image management says:
“Protect your reputation.”
The Gospel says:
“Confess and receive mercy.”
Image management says:
“Hide the scandal.”
Jesus says:
“Give Me the sinner.”
And at Calvary, the sinless Christ carried the judgment sinners deserved.
He was crucified.
Buried.
And He rose.
So the deepest message of this article is not:
“Try harder not to lust.”
It is:
Run to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the fantasy.
Bring Him the pornography.
Bring Him the emotional affair.
Bring Him the wandering eyes.
Bring Him the imagination you cannot seem to control.
Bring Him your shame.
Bring Him your excuses.
Bring Him your failures.
And then keep bringing your mind under His lordship.
Not once.
Again tomorrow.
Again when temptation comes.
Again when you feel weak.
Again when the old images return.
Again when you realize holiness is not accomplished in one emotional night but formed through thousands of surrendered moments.
The goal is not merely to become someone who can say:
“I never physically cheated.”
The goal is to become someone whose secret life increasingly belongs to Jesus.
Maybe nobody else knows why you needed this article.
God does.
And perhaps your next act of worship is not another song.
Perhaps it is honesty.
Not because strangers need the details.
They do not.
You do not owe the internet your private confession.
But sometimes three simple words become a line in the sand:
No more hiding.
Your testimony may become the reason another believer realizes they are not the only person fighting in secret.
And please—do not merely read this and disappear.
Ask Jesus about you.
About your eyes.
Your thoughts.
Your habits.
Your imagination.
Your hidden rooms.
Because physical faithfulness is beautiful.
But Christ wants more than behavior that survives public inspection.
He wants the heart.
And when you finally hand Him the room you were most ashamed to open, you may discover that the place you expected Him to abandon you becomes the very place where His transforming grace meets you.
Jesus does not expose the hidden room to destroy you; He turns on the light because He intends to lead you out.
